Reconcile

/REK-un-syl/ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Reconcile means to restore a friendly relationship after a quarrel or disagreement; it can also mean to make two ideas or accounts consistent with each other.

Two sisters who had not spoken since an argument over their grandmother's house finally chose to reconcile at their niece's wedding, hugging before the first dance.

Worked Example

After splitting up over creative differences a decade ago, the two bandmates reconciled and agreed to play one final charity concert together.

The bandmates had a broken relationship, and they repaired it — they came back together on friendly terms. That act of restoring a damaged bond is exactly what reconcile names.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

make up: To make up is the informal, everyday way to say two people became friendly again after a fight — schoolyard quarrels, roommate spats. Reconcile is the formal register for the same repair, the word for estranged siblings, divided families, and warring parties.

mend: To mend is to repair something damaged, and it needs that damaged thing as its object — you mend a torn sleeve or a strained friendship. Reconcile can stand on its own: after years of silence, two people simply reconcile, no object required.

settle: To settle is to resolve the dispute itself — you settle an argument, a lawsuit, a question — and once terms are fixed, the matter is closed. To reconcile is to restore the relationship between the people, which can stay broken long after the issue is settled.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

feud: to carry on a long, bitter quarrel

alienate: to drive someone away or make them hostile

Where it sits · how fully the bond is repaired — coexist → reconcile → reunite

coexist vs. reconcile: Coexist is weaker than reconcile — neighbors who merely coexist avoid open conflict, but nothing warm between them has been repaired.

reunite vs. reconcile: Reunite is stronger than reconcile — friends who reunite don't just make peace; they come back together as if the split had never happened.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — re-

Prefix — re-: again, back

Root — concile

Root — concile: to bring together, win over (Latin conciliare, from concilium, an assembly or gathering)

Put it together

Put it together: To reconcile is literally to 'bring together again.' The Latin root pictures people being called back into one assembly after they had drifted apart.

Use the root in a new word: irreconcilable

Use the root in a new word: irreconcilable: Their views on the budget seemed irreconcilable until a fresh proposal finally satisfied both of them.

Root Check

Word Choice

Neutral — everyday and formal use

The primary sense is about people returning to harmony after a dispute. A second sense means making ideas or records consistent: you can reconcile a bank statement with your receipts, or reconcile new evidence with an old theory. Related adjective form: conciliatory, which describes a friendly tone or gesture aimed at ending a dispute — a conciliatory apology can be the first step before two people fully reconcile.
